newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean doctors say Tutsi rebels kill 34 patients.
newsitem.headline: Zairean doctors say Tutsi rebels kill 34 patients.

text.p: Zairean doctors said on Wednesday ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels slaughtered 34 patients and six staff at a hospital in eastern Zaire last weekend.

In the border town of Bukavu on Wednesday, witnesses said Zairean security forces prepared on Wednesday for a clampdown on Banyamulenge, confiscating aid agency vehicles after the estimated 200,000 Banyamulenge were given a week to leave.
Two doctors told reporters in Bukavu some 100 Banyamulenge fighters attacked the hospital in Lemera town about 60 km (40 miles) to the south from Sunday night for about eight hours.
"The Banyamulenge arrived at the hospital and opened fire. They killed 28 patients in their beds, 34 patients in all, and four male nurses and two doctors," Dr Aubin Mulaga said.
The doctors said the Banyamulenge gunmen attacked because the hospital was treating Hutu war wounded from the conflict between the Zairean army, Banyamulenge and local Zairean tribes.
"We are medical persons and we don't have the right to distinguish between patients. But it is true we had Hutu wounded and no Banyamulenge patients," said Mulaga who escaped unharmed.
A U.N. official confirmed the attack on the 360-bed Lemera hospital, one of the best in the region, saying armed men said to be Banyamulenge killed patients and damaged a generator.
Aid workers said they feared all-out war would break out in the region after the one-week ultimatum for the Banyamulenge to leave their home area south of Bukavu or be treated as rebels.
"We fear there will be a fully-fledged war with helicopter gunships and heavy arms being used by the Zaireans after the people leave," said an aid worker.
"The situation is explosive," added a U.N. official.
South Kivu Deputy Governor Lwasi Ngabo Lwabanji issued the ultimatum on Tuesday and told a news conference in Bukavu the Banyamulenge Tutsis were bent on destabilising eastern Zaire.
He said rebels, with hundreds of thousands of Banyamulenge civilians living in the plateau area of South Kivu, had a week to leave or face all-out war from the Zairean defence forces.
He said any Banyamulenge failing to heed his warning within seven days would be considered rebels and attacked by troops.
"We are opening a corridor for the Banyamulenge who want to get out for one week. After that whoever remains will be considered a rebel and will be treated as such," he said.

Conflict between the army and estimated 200,000 Banyamulenge has been growing for months. The Banyamulenge are ethnic Tutsis who arrived up to 200 years ago from what are now neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi.

Zairean authorities have whipped up public opinion against the Banyamulenge and diplomats fear conflict could spread as the mainly Tutsi armies in Rwanda and Burundi may decide to support their kinfolk.
Zairean authorities want to concentrate the Banyamulenge in government-controlled camps to make them easier to monitor.
On Tuesday Bukavu was shaken by more than an hour of gunfire by Zairean troops after the bodies of an army colonel and six soldiers killed in fighting with Banyamulenge arrived in town.
Zairean soldiers went on a looting rampage in Uvira town for about four hours on Tuesday, robbing foreign aid workers at gunpoint and stealing at least two aid vehicles, residents said.
Zaire's army is notoriously indisciplined. Soldiers say their pay is a pittance and they turn to crime to survive.
But their commander-in-chief, President Mobutu Sese Seko, is not in the country to impose his limited authority. Mobutu is in Switzerland after surgery with no firm date for his return.
